reception.text: The Associated Press carried the order the day it was issued, under a head calling it a reorganization of the consular service "on a Merit Basis and Divorced from Political Party Affiliations," and summarized the promotion rule, the 80 per cent passing mark and the age limits.

political_impact.text: The order put the consular service on a merit footing, carrying out the consular reorganization act of April 5, 1906, with a Board of Examiners and written examinations.

legacy.text: Amended repeatedly and by the act of May 21, 1908, the consular merit system pointed toward the career Foreign Service built by the Rogers Act of 1924.

legacy.text: The board was abolished in 1934 rather than reconstituted; the modern U.S. Board on Geographic Names was created by Congress in 1947 and extended to foreign names.
The advisory power over federal mapmaking passed in 1919 to a newly created Board of Surveys and Maps, set up for the same purpose of coordinating map-making agencies and avoiding duplicated work.

today.name: United States Geographic Board
today.note: Abolished in 1934; functions moved to the Interior Department.

related.note: January 1906 order giving the Board on Geographic Names added duties.

later_actions.text: Executive Order 3206 rescinded the 1906 advisory powers over mapmaking and transferred them to the new Board of Surveys and Maps, later the Federal Board of Surveys and Maps.
Executive Order 6680 abolished the United States Geographic Board, moving its functions, staff, records and funds to the Interior Department and revoking the 1890 founding order.
Congress created the United States Board on Geographic Names by statute.

political_impact.text: The Reclamation Service reported a quarter-section on the Belle Fourche project set aside for an experimental farm, fenced and partly plowed, with experiments run by the Department of Agriculture; this is probably the land the order reserved.

legacy.text: The Belle Fourche Experiment Farm, about two miles northwest of Newell, carried on cereal work from 1907.

political_impact.text: The withdrawal held land while Congress passed the act of June 27, 1906, letting Wisconsin select up to twenty thousand acres of public land for forestry.
political_impact.source: Decisions Relating to the Public Lands, vol. 35, p. 11

legacy.text: The withdrawal lapsed on its own terms, but the twenty thousand acres it protected went to the State of Wisconsin for forestry.
